propositions.text: Whether toxic psychosis from self-induced intoxication is a 'mental disorder' under s.16 Cr. C. exempting appellant from criminal responsibility
Review scope of insanity defence and defence of self-induced intoxication

paragraphs.summary: The court must decide if toxic psychosis from self-induced intoxication is a 'mental disorder' under s.16 Cr. C. and review insanity and intoxication defences.

propositions.text: Appellant assaulted two individuals in psychotic condition caused by drugs, seriously injuring one by stomping on his head
Appellant convicted by Court of Québec on aggravated assault and assault charges
Appellant unsuccessfully appealed for not criminally responsible verdict on mental disorder grounds
Appellant now appeals Quebec Court of Appeal judgment rejecting toxic psychosis as 'mental disorder' under s.16 Cr. C.

paragraphs.summary: The appellant assaulted two people in drug-induced psychosis, was convicted, unsuccessfully appealed, and now appeals the Court of Appeal's rejection of his mental disorder defence.

propositions.text: Judgment of Court of Appeal is correct in law
Appeal should be dismissed

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the Court of Appeal's judgment correct and dismisses the appeal.

propositions.text: Appellant and acquaintance smoked marijuana and took amphetamines on October 23, 2005
They traveled by bus from Rivière-du-Loup to Mont-Joli while still intoxicated

paragraphs.summary: The appellant and acquaintance used marijuana and amphetamines and traveled intoxicated by bus on October 23, 2005.

propositions.text: Appellant and friend hitchhiked to Amqui; picked up by Gilles Tremblay at 1:30 a.m.
No signs of intoxication apparent during car trip; witnesses said appellant was 'OK' near Val-Brillant
Drugs taken on October 23 had ceased effect before arrival in Amqui

paragraphs.summary: Appellant hitchhiked to Amqui, showed no intoxication signs during car trip, and drugs taken earlier had ceased effect.

propositions.text: In Amqui, appellant and friend bought and took 'poire bleue' ecstasy pills on October 24 night
They decided to attack Dany Lévesque for real or imagined reason of his 'upside-down cross' necklace
At 5:00 a.m., they illegally entered Lévesque's building and attacked him

paragraphs.summary: Appellant and friend took ecstasy pills, decided to attack Lévesque over 'upside-down cross', and illegally entered his building to assault him.

propositions.text: Roger Dumas tried to intervene during attack; appellant threw him down stairs and stomped on his head
Dumas was disabled and will require lifelong hospital care

paragraphs.summary: Dumas tried to intervene but was thrown down stairs and stomped on, resulting in lifelong disability.

propositions.text: Appellant was highly intoxicated from 'poire bleue' pill effects at time of assault
Pill caused dissociation between appellant's perceptions and reality; witnesses said he acted 'weird' and 'out of it'

paragraphs.summary: Appellant was highly intoxicated from the pill, causing dissociation and odd behaviour noted by witnesses.

propositions.text: Appellant experienced religious delirium after taking drug, obsessed with 'upside-down cross'
During attack, made absurd religious statements and gestures, then left calmly

paragraphs.summary: Appellant had religious delirium with absurd statements during attack and left calmly afterwards.

propositions.text: No dispute appellant was in serious psychotic condition at offence time, effects ended by October 28, 2005
How psychosis affects appellant's criminal responsibility is essential issue
Appellant had no prior psychotic episodes, no underlying mental disease, no addiction, and was occasional drug user

paragraphs.summary: Appellant was in serious psychosis with no prior episodes or addiction; key issue is effect on criminal responsibility.

propositions.text: Appellant charged with aggravated assault, assault, breaking and entering with intent, and attempted break-in
Appellant pleaded not guilty to all charges

paragraphs.summary: Appellant was charged with multiple offences and pleaded not guilty.

propositions.text: At trial, appellant raised defence of psychotic condition induced by friend's spiritual influence
Psychotic condition prevented appellant from judging drug-taking impact, exempting him from liability

paragraphs.summary: At trial, appellant claimed psychosis from friend's spiritual influence exempted him from liability.

propositions.text: Two psychiatrists agreed appellant was in severe psychosis unable to distinguish right from wrong
Defence expert said psychosis mainly from mystical influence, drug-taking decision not free
Crown expert said no third-party influence; psychosis caused by toxic substances

paragraphs.summary: Experts agreed appellant was psychotic; defence said mystical influence caused it, Crown said toxic substances caused it.

propositions.text: Judge Decoste accepted Crown expert's opinion that appellant had toxic psychosis
Appellant acquitted on breaking and entering charges due to extreme intoxication
Appellant convicted on aggravated assault and assault, relying on s.33.1 Cr. C. barring intoxication defence for bodily harm offences

paragraphs.summary: Trial judge found toxic psychosis, acquitted appellant on break-in charges, convicted on assaults citing s.33.1 Cr. C.

propositions.text: Judge Decoste sentenced appellant to five years for aggravated assault and three months concurrent for assault

paragraphs.summary: Trial judge sentenced appellant to five years for aggravated assault and three months concurrent for assault.

propositions.text: Appellant appealed guilty verdict and sentence to Quebec Court of Appeal
Appellant changed defence, conceding toxic psychosis but claiming mental disorder defence under s.16 Cr. C.

paragraphs.summary: Appellant appealed and changed defence to claim mental disorder under s.16 Cr. C. due to toxic psychosis.

propositions.text: Trial judge confused insanity defence under s.16 Cr. C. with self-induced intoxication defence under s.33.1 Cr. C.
Appellant asked Court of Appeal to disregard s.33.1 and find toxic psychosis a 'mental disorder' under s.16 Cr. C.

paragraphs.summary: Appellant argued trial judge confused defences and asked Court of Appeal to find toxic psychosis a 'mental disorder' under s.16 Cr. C.

propositions.text: Court of Appeal disagreed psychotic condition was unforeseeable; expert evidence showed high risk of psychosis from drugs
Appellant seemed to be among those likely to develop psychosis, lasting as long as intoxication

paragraphs.summary: Court of Appeal found psychosis was foreseeable and appellant was likely to develop it lasting as long as intoxication.

propositions.text: Defence of self-induced intoxication available in extreme cases for general intent offences per R. v. Daviault
Parliament limited this defence to non-violent offences by s.33.1 Cr. C.

paragraphs.summary: Court of Appeal noted self-induced intoxication defence is limited to non-violent offences by s.33.1 Cr. C.

propositions.text: Insanity defence under s.16 Cr. C. applies to underlying mental disorder worsened by drug use
Cooper v. The Queen held transitory drug-induced psychosis is not a 'disease of the mind' under ss.2 and 16 Cr. C.
Court of Appeal held appellant's toxic psychosis did not qualify for insanity defence under s.16 Cr. C.

paragraphs.summary: Court of Appeal held transitory drug-induced psychosis is not a 'disease of the mind' and denied insanity defence under s.16 Cr. C.

propositions.text: Thibault J.A. found appellant had no underlying disease of mind and became sane after effects of 'poire bleue' passed
Appellant's argument was an attempt to circumvent Parliament's intent to preclude self-induced intoxication defence for bodily integrity offences

paragraphs.summary: Thibault J.A. found appellant had no underlying mental disease and argued appellant tried to circumvent Parliament's intent on intoxication defence.

propositions.text: Court of Appeal dismissed appeal against sentence as sentences were harsh but not unreasonable

paragraphs.summary: Court of Appeal dismissed appeal against sentence as sentences were harsh but not unreasonable.

propositions.text: Does s. 33.1 Cr. C. limit scope of defence of not criminally responsible on account of mental disorder under s. 16 Cr. C.?
Can toxic psychosis caused by self-induced intoxication be a 'mental disorder' under s. 16 Cr. C.?

paragraphs.summary: Court identifies two issues: whether s. 33.1 limits s. 16 defence and if toxic psychosis from intoxication is a 'mental disorder'.

propositions.text: Appellant concedes toxic psychosis resulted exclusively from self-induced intoxication on October 24, 2005
Appellant disagrees courts failed to consider predisposition to psychiatric disorder but does not argue intoxication triggered latent disease
Appellant's counsel stated not raising latent disease ground of appeal

paragraphs.summary: Appellant concedes toxic psychosis from intoxication, disagrees on predisposition consideration, but does not appeal latent disease argument.

propositions.text: Appellant argues single intoxication episode causing toxic psychosis can be 'mental disorder' under s. 16 Cr. C.
Appellant's syllogism: toxic psychosis affects only fragile psyches, so legally it is a mental disorder

paragraphs.summary: Appellant argues toxic psychosis from single intoxication episode is a 'mental disorder' legally because it affects vulnerable individuals.

propositions.text: Appellant argues toxic psychosis results from underlying disease of mind revealed by intoxication
Due to evidence and trial findings, appellant relies on general argument that any toxic psychosis is a 'mental disorder' under s. 16 Cr. C.
Appellant premises that intoxication cannot be real cause of toxic psychosis; it must originate in pre-existing condition

paragraphs.summary: Appellant argues toxic psychosis stems from underlying disease, relying on general claim that all toxic psychosis is a 'mental disorder'.

propositions.text: Appellant contends psychotic condition legally means not merely intoxicated
Appellant argues Court of Appeal confused self-induced intoxication defence with mental disorder defence under s. 16 Cr. C.
Appellant says Thibault J.A. erred in stating s. 33.1 Cr. C. prevents intoxication defence and limits mental disorder defence

paragraphs.summary: Appellant argues psychosis means not mere intoxication and Court of Appeal confused intoxication and mental disorder defences.

propositions.text: Appellant says s. 33.1 Cr. C. endorses dissent in Daviault that self-induced intoxication defence unavailable for general intent offences
Dissent in Daviault acknowledged toxic psychosis remains defence under s. 16 Cr. C.
Appellant submits dissent balanced punishing voluntary intoxication but protecting those lacking mental capacity
Appellant cites Sopinka J. dissent that intoxication-induced mental illness affects fragile individuals
Appellant raises no constitutional challenge to s. 33.1 Cr. C., only interpretation and application issues

paragraphs.summary: Appellant argues s. 33.1 Cr. C. endorses Daviault dissent that toxic psychosis is defence, raising no constitutional issues.

propositions.text: Three seminal cases led to enactment of s. 33.1 Cr. C., starting with House of Lords decision in DPP v. Beard
Beard set three rules on intoxication as insanity defence and specific intent offences

paragraphs.summary: Court summarizes seminal cases leading to s. 33.1 Cr. C., starting with Beard's three intoxication rules.

propositions.text: Beard principle: intoxication can be defence for specific intent offences in certain circumstances
Robinson modified Beard's third rule, requiring actual specific intent for intoxication defence under Charter

paragraphs.summary: Court explains Beard principle on intoxication defence and Robinson's modification under Charter rights.

propositions.text: Since Beard, intoxication defence applies to specific intent offences or lesser general intent offences
Leary held self-induced intoxication cannot raise reasonable doubt for general intent offences
Leary rule: recklessness in voluntary intoxication suffices for general intent offence fault element

paragraphs.summary: Court outlines intoxication defence evolution: Beard, Leary's rejection for general intent, and recklessness standard.

propositions.text: Daviault majority held Leary rule violated Charter for general intent offences
Daviault established intoxication causing automatism or insanity state can raise reasonable doubt for general intent offences

paragraphs.summary: Daviault majority held Leary rule unconstitutional and allowed intoxication-induced automatism defence for general intent offences.

propositions.text: Sopinka J. dissented in Daviault, supporting Leary rule and society's right to punish voluntary intoxication

paragraphs.summary: Sopinka J. dissented in Daviault, supporting Leary rule and punishing voluntary intoxication.

propositions.text: Parliament enacted s. 33.1 Cr. C. less than a year after Daviault to prevent intoxication defence for general intent violent crimes
Section 33.1 Cr. C. prohibits defence of self-induced intoxication for offences involving bodily integrity interference

paragraphs.summary: Parliament enacted s. 33.1 Cr. C. to bar intoxication defence for violent crimes involving bodily integrity.

propositions.text: Appellant argues Parliament implicitly endorsed Sopinka J.'s dissent by enacting s. 33.1 Cr. C.
Enactment of s. 33.1 Cr. C. limited majority rule in Daviault, not reviving Leary rule or dissent position
Daviault principles remain law except for s. 33.1 Cr. C. restriction
Appellant's acquittal on property offences shows Daviault still applies outside s. 33.1 Cr. C. scope

paragraphs.summary: Court finds s. 33.1 Cr. C. limits Daviault majority rule but does not revive Leary; appellant's acquittal shows Daviault still applies.

propositions.text: s. 33.1 Cr. C. should not be interpreted to limit scope of s. 16 Cr. C. defence
Intoxication and insanity are distinct legal concepts with different defences and principles

paragraphs.summary: Court finds s. 33.1 Cr. C. should not limit s. 16 Cr. C. defence; intoxication and insanity are distinct concepts.

propositions.text: Application of s. 16 Cr. C. and s. 33.1 Cr. C. are mutually exclusive
If accused lacked general intent due to intoxication, incapacity not caused by disease of mind (R. v. Huppie)
If accused was intoxicated but incapable due to mental disorder, s. 33.1 Cr. C. does not apply

paragraphs.summary: Court states s. 16 and s. 33.1 Cr. C. defences are mutually exclusive with legal precedents.

propositions.text: Court must identify source of psychosis: self-induced intoxication or disease of mind to determine applicable defence
Identification is difficult if mental health was precarious before intoxication
Source identification determines criminal responsibility

paragraphs.summary: Court explains importance and difficulty of identifying psychosis source to determine criminal responsibility.

propositions.text: Legal concept of 'disease of the mind' excludes self-induced states and transitory mental states (Cooper)

paragraphs.summary: Court cites Cooper defining 'disease of the mind' excluding self-induced and transitory states.

propositions.text: Correlation exists between self-induced states excluded from 'disease of mind' and intoxication states covered by s. 33.1 Cr. C.
Court must first consider insanity defence under s. 16 Cr. C. before considering s. 33.1 Cr. C.
Starting analysis with s. 33.1 Cr. C. would reverse proper legal process and confuse causation issues

paragraphs.summary: Court instructs to analyze s. 16 insanity defence before s. 33.1 intoxication defence to maintain proper legal process.

propositions.text: Appellant argues Cooper's exclusion of self-induced intoxication states applies only to normal intoxication effects.
Whether toxic psychosis from intoxication is a mental disorder under s.16 Cr. C. or excluded by Cooper.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the appellant argues Cooper's exclusion applies only to normal intoxication effects and raises the issue whether toxic psychosis is a mental disorder under s.16 Cr. C.

propositions.text: Court will examine Cooper's exclusion scope later.
Appellant's criticism of Court of Appeal's position on ss.16 and 33.1 Cr. C. interplay is unfounded.
Thibault J.A. stated no overlap possible between ss.16 and 33.1 Cr. C.; psychosis from drug consumption excludes s.16 application.
Appellant was legally intoxicated at material time.
Appellant's argument indirectly avoids s.33.1 Cr. C. application.

paragraphs.summary: The court will later examine Cooper's exclusion, finds appellant's criticism unfounded, and reports Thibault J.A.'s findings on ss.16 and 33.1 Cr. C. and appellant's intoxication.

propositions.text: Whether Court of Appeal erred in applying s.33.1 Cr. C. instead of s.16 Cr. C.
Court will consider legal principles and policy underlying s.16 Cr. C. defence.

paragraphs.summary: The court identifies the issue of whether the Court of Appeal erred applying s.33.1 Cr. C. and will consider legal principles of s.16 Cr. C.

propositions.text: Defence of not criminally responsible on mental disorder protects criminal justice system integrity and fundamental principles.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the defence protects the criminal justice system's integrity and fundamental principles.

propositions.text: Criminal responsibility requires commission of a voluntary act.
Principle based on fairness to avoid punishing involuntary acts.

paragraphs.summary: The court states criminal responsibility requires a voluntary act, based on fairness to avoid punishing involuntary acts.

propositions.text: Voluntary act must be product of free will (R. v. King).
No criminal responsibility for involuntary acts (Rabey dissent, endorsed in Parks).

paragraphs.summary: The court cites law that voluntary acts require free will and no responsibility for involuntary acts.

propositions.text: Will expressed through conscious physical or moral control (Perka, Parent).

paragraphs.summary: The court states will is expressed through conscious physical or moral control over actions.

propositions.text: Criminal law views individuals as autonomous, rational beings; voluntary acts reflect free will and reason (Perka, Alexander & Ferzan, Ruzic).

paragraphs.summary: The court explains criminal law views individuals as autonomous and rational; voluntary acts reflect free will and reason.

propositions.text: Presumption of autonomy and rationality can be rebutted by proof of incapacity at material time (Chaulk, Ruzic).

paragraphs.summary: The court states the presumption of autonomy can be rebutted by proof of incapacity at the material time.

propositions.text: Insanity is exception; mental disorder means incapacity to appreciate nature or wrongness of acts (Chaulk).

paragraphs.summary: The court states insanity is an exception where mental disorder means incapacity to appreciate nature or wrongness of acts.

propositions.text: Insane person incapable of morally voluntary conduct; conviction would undermine criminal law foundations (Ruzic logic).

paragraphs.summary: The court states insane persons lack moral voluntariness; convicting them undermines criminal law foundations.

propositions.text: Mental disorder defence leads to not criminally responsible verdict triggering administrative process for public safety and care.

paragraphs.summary: The court states mental disorder defence leads to not criminally responsible verdict triggering administrative process for safety and care.

propositions.text: Part XX.1 Criminal Code scheme replaces common law for mentally ill offenders (Swain, Winko).
NCR accused found not criminally responsible triggers assessment of dangerousness and treatment needs (Winko).

paragraphs.summary: The court explains Part XX.1 replaces common law for mentally ill offenders and triggers assessment of dangerousness and treatment.

propositions.text: Court will review s.16 Cr. C. conditions and consider toxic psychoses from self-induced intoxication.

paragraphs.summary: The court will review s.16 Cr. C. conditions and consider toxic psychoses from self-induced intoxication.

propositions.text: Accused presumed not to suffer mental disorder exempting criminal responsibility; must prove on balance of probabilities (s.16(2), Chaulk).

paragraphs.summary: The court states accused must prove mental disorder exempting responsibility on balance of probabilities despite presumption otherwise.

propositions.text: Two-stage test: mental disorder existence and incapacity to know act was wrong (s.16(1)).

paragraphs.summary: The court states the two-stage test for mental disorder defence: existence and incapacity to know wrongness.

propositions.text: No dispute appellant was incapable of distinguishing right from wrong at material time.
Trial judge found appellant in serious psychotic condition and unaware of actions (para. 2).
Only issue is whether psychosis resulted from mental disorder under s.16 Cr. C.

paragraphs.summary: The court states no dispute appellant was psychotic and unaware; issue is whether psychosis is mental disorder under s.16.

propositions.text: Criminal Code defines mental disorder as 'disease of the mind' without precise definition.
Courts have delineated legal concept over time due to circular definition.

paragraphs.summary: The court states Criminal Code defines mental disorder as 'disease of the mind' and courts have delineated the concept over time.

propositions.text: Cooper defines 'disease of the mind' broadly as any illness impairing mind functioning.
Rabey confirms broad concept includes organic and functional disorders, curable or not.
Definition's inclusiveness explained by Parliament's wish to protect public from threats.

paragraphs.summary: The court states Cooper and Rabey define 'disease of the mind' broadly, reflecting Parliament's public protection intent.

propositions.text: Mental disorder concept evolves with medical science and is not precisely definable (Simpson, Rabey).
Concept is flexible to apply to recognized disorders impairing mind and compatible with s.16 policy.

paragraphs.summary: The court states mental disorder concept evolves with science, is flexible, and not precisely definable.

propositions.text: “Disease of the mind” is a legal concept with a medical dimension under the Criminal Code.
Whether a mental condition is a “mental disorder” is a question of law for the trial judge, not the jury.
Psychiatrists describe mental condition medically; judge decides if it fits “disease of the mind” legally (Simpson).
If judge finds mental condition is a “mental disorder”, jury decides if accused had it at offence time.

paragraphs.summary: The court explains that “disease of the mind” is a legal concept decided by the judge, with medical input from psychiatrists, and jury decides factual presence.

propositions.text: Trial judge is not bound by medical evidence as experts ignore policy aspects of s.16 Cr.C.
Expert opinion on whether mental condition is a “mental disorder” has little evidentiary value (R. v. Luedecke).

paragraphs.summary: The court states the trial judge is not bound by medical evidence and expert opinion on legal issue has little evidentiary value.

propositions.text: Mental conditions included in “disease of the mind” is a question of law; whether accused’s condition meets test is mixed law and fact; whether accused suffered disease is fact for trier of fact (R. v. Stone).

paragraphs.summary: The court cites Stone that defining “disease of the mind” is law, applying it is mixed law and fact, and actual suffering is fact for trier of fact.

propositions.text: Central issue is whether toxic psychosis from single intoxication episode is a “mental disorder” under s.16 Cr.C.
It is agreed appellant was psychotic and unable to distinguish right from wrong at offence time.

paragraphs.summary: The court identifies the issue as whether toxic psychosis from single intoxication is a “mental disorder”, noting appellant was psychotic then.

propositions.text: Toxic psychosis must always be considered a “mental disorder”.
Appellant’s argument wrongly makes legal characterization depend solely on medical diagnosis, shifting decision from judge/jury to expert.
Appellant’s argument conflicts with three decades of case law and cannot succeed.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds appellant’s argument that toxic psychosis is always a “mental disorder” conflicts with case law and wrongly shifts legal decision to experts.

propositions.text: “Toxic psychosis” is medically diagnosed but its causes vary widely and are not always precisely identified.
Case law shows toxic psychosis arises in diverse circumstances related to toxic substance exposure.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds toxic psychosis is medically diagnosed but its causes vary widely, as shown by case law.

propositions.text: Many factors contribute to substance-induced psychosis, including personality disorders, stress, drug dependence, heavy use, and withdrawal.
Diversity arises from psychological makeup, histories, drug nature, quantity, and toxicity.
Each case depends on its own facts and cannot always fit existing case law easily.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds many factors contribute to toxic psychosis and each case depends on unique facts, defying easy categorization.

propositions.text: It is unwise to adopt appellant’s broad approach to toxic psychosis as always a “mental disorder”.
Cooper urges caution with intoxication-related mental conditions and recommends a contextual approach balancing public protection and criminal liability.
Contextual approach requires case-specific analysis; recent decisions suggesting toxic psychosis always a disease of mind are rejected.

paragraphs.summary: The court rejects appellant’s broad approach, endorses Cooper’s contextual approach, and rejects recent decisions treating toxic psychosis as always a disease of mind.

propositions.text: General principle: temporary psychosis from intoxication is excluded by Cooper.
Accused can rebut presumption by showing disease of mind unrelated to intoxication symptoms at offence time.
Court should adopt Stone’s “more holistic approach” to determine if accused’s mental condition is a “mental disorder”.
Attorney General of Ontario supports holistic approach to determine mental disorder under s.16 Cr.C.

paragraphs.summary: The court states Cooper excludes temporary intoxication psychosis, but accused can rebut by showing unrelated disease using Stone’s holistic approach, supported by Ontario AG.

propositions.text: Stone proposes flexible approach with two analytical tools and policy considerations to distinguish mental disorders from intoxication states.
Approach helps determine if medically diagnosed disease of mind is a legal mental disorder under s.16 Cr.C.

paragraphs.summary: The court explains Stone’s flexible approach with analytical tools and policy considerations to distinguish legal mental disorders from intoxication states.

propositions.text: Internal cause factor compares accused to normal person to see if trigger would cause automatism in normal person (Stone).
If normal person might react similarly, trigger is external and excludes condition from s.16 Cr.C. mental disorder scope.

paragraphs.summary: The court explains Stone’s internal cause factor compares accused to normal person to determine if trigger is external, excluding mental disorder.

propositions.text: Trigger can be alcohol or drug use; court must consider all consumption circumstances to assess normal person’s reaction.
If normal person might develop toxic psychosis from similar drug use, accused’s condition is external and not a disease of mind (Rabey, Moroz).

paragraphs.summary: The court states trigger may be drug use; if normal person might develop toxic psychosis similarly, accused’s condition is external and not a disease of mind.

propositions.text: Continuing danger factor assesses likelihood of recurring danger to others to determine disease of mind (Stone).
Court considers psychiatric history and likelihood trigger will recur to assess danger.

paragraphs.summary: The court explains Stone’s continuing danger factor assesses recurring danger likelihood using psychiatric history and trigger recurrence.

propositions.text: Recurring danger must arise independently of accused’s will; voluntary future danger from drug use is not a mental disorder under s.16 Cr.C.
Mental disorder defence applies to morally involuntary actions and inherent dangers persisting despite accused’s will.

paragraphs.summary: The court states recurring danger must be independent of accused’s will; voluntary future danger from drugs is not a mental disorder.

propositions.text: Holistic approach allows judges to consider policy concerns, mainly protecting society via Part XX.1 of Criminal Code (Stone).
If pre-existing condition needs no treatment and poses no threat, court should more easily find no disease of mind.

paragraphs.summary: The court explains Stone’s holistic approach includes policy concerns like public protection and no disease if no treatment or threat needed.

propositions.text: Contextual approach defines appeal scope; no universal rule for toxic psychosis cases; focus on single episode self-induced intoxication.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the appeal concerns only toxic psychosis from single self-induced intoxication episode, not all cases.

propositions.text: Courts should apply Stone’s holistic approach case-by-case to determine if mental condition fits Cooper’s disease of mind definition.
This approach aligns with Rabey endorsing case-by-case analysis for transient mental disturbances.

paragraphs.summary: The court directs courts to apply Stone’s holistic approach case-by-case, consistent with Rabey, for transient mental disturbances.

propositions.text: Court will determine if appellant had a “mental disorder” under s.16 Cr.C. using trial judge’s findings.
Trial judge found appellant highly intoxicated and psychotic from voluntary drug use at offence time.
Appellant argues toxic psychosis is necessarily a “mental disorder” as an abnormal intoxication effect affecting predisposed or fragile psyches.

paragraphs.summary: The court will decide if appellant had a mental disorder using trial judge’s findings; appellant argues toxic psychosis is always a mental disorder.

propositions.text: Evidence does not support appellant’s distinction between normal and abnormal intoxication effects.
Evidence does not support that only predisposed persons develop toxic psychosis from drug use.
Dr. Faucher testified toxic psychosis cases occur weekly; 50% of PCP users likely develop psychosis when intoxicated.
Thibault J.A. noted Dr. Faucher’s testimony on toxic psychosis frequency and PCP effects.
Toxic psychosis is a frequent phenomenon resulting from high toxicity of chemical drugs.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds evidence and expert testimony show toxic psychosis is frequent and not limited to predisposed persons.

propositions.text: Stone’s first factor suggests a normal person would likely develop toxic psychosis from one “poire bleue” pill.
This suggests appellant was not suffering from a mental disorder at offence time.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds that a normal person would likely develop toxic psychosis from the pill, suggesting appellant had no mental disorder.

propositions.text: Rapid psychotic symptoms indicate delusions are due to a specific external factor, like self-induced intoxication.
Dr. Faucher's assessment, preferred over Dr. Turmel's, shows rapid symptom reversal is typical of toxic psychosis from self-intoxication.
Professor Parent states delusions subsiding with drug effects usually indicate substance intoxication, not a disease of the mind.
Such delusions do not result from a disease of the mind under the Criminal Code.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds rapid psychotic symptoms indicate toxic psychosis from self-intoxication, not a disease of the mind under the Criminal Code.

propositions.text: Appellant's psychotic symptoms diminished after taking 'poire bleue' pill and disappeared by October 28, 2005.
Court of Appeal held symptom disappearance showed toxic psychosis coincided with intoxication duration.
Thibault J.A. said appellant had no disease of the mind before crimes and was sane after drug effects passed.
No valid reason to depart from Court of Appeal's conclusion on appellant's sanity after intoxication effects passed.

paragraphs.summary: The court agrees with the Court of Appeal that appellant's symptoms matched intoxication duration and he was sane after effects passed.

propositions.text: No evidence shows appellant's mental condition is inherently dangerous.
If appellant abstains voluntarily from drugs, his mental condition poses no public safety threat.
If appellant had drug dependency impairing voluntary abstinence, risk of recurring danger might be greater.
Court will not adopt a definitive position on danger without evidence of dependency.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds no evidence of inherent danger in appellant's mental condition if he abstains voluntarily from drugs.

propositions.text: No valid reason to initiate special procedure under Part XX.1 of the Criminal Code.
Accused with mental condition solely from temporary self-induced intoxication and no threat is not suffering from 'mental disorder' under s.16 Cr. C.
Part XX.1 applies only if accused actually suffered from a disease of the mind at the material time.
Part XX.1 not intended for accused with temporary madness induced artificially by intoxication.

paragraphs.summary: The court concludes Part XX.1 does not apply to accused with mental condition solely from self-induced intoxication and no threat.

propositions.text: Appellant was not suffering from a 'mental disorder' under s.16 Cr. C. at assault time.
Appellant failed to rebut presumption that toxic psychosis was self-induced by alcohol or drugs per Cooper definition.
Malfunctioning mind from self-induced intoxication is not a legal disease of the mind as not from inherent psychological makeup.
Medical science may consider such conditions diseases, but legally toxic psychosis is a symptom of intoxication state.
Such state cannot justify exempting accused from criminal responsibility under s.16 Cr. C.

paragraphs.summary: The court concludes appellant's toxic psychosis was self-induced and not a legal mental disorder exempting criminal responsibility.

propositions.text: Conclusion aligns with policy considerations from Dickson J. in Cooper.
Dr. Faucher's assessment shows toxic psychosis frequency in similar cases.
Appellant's position would broaden s.16 Cr. C. defence beyond Parliament's intent if adopted.
Defence scope would be unacceptably broad if toxic psychosis always excused criminal responsibility.
Toxic psychosis here is covered by Cooper's exclusion of self-induced states caused by alcohol or drugs.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds adopting appellant's position would unacceptably broaden s.16 defence; toxic psychosis is excluded as self-induced.

propositions.text: No evidence appellant suffered underlying mental disorder simplifies legal characterization under s.16 Cr. C.
Factual case is clear: appellant's condition covered by Cooper's exclusion, like in Paul.
Appellant asks court to assume toxic psychosis caused by underlying mental disorder without evidence.
Unreasonable to assume underlying disorder absent evidence.
No Canadian court applied s.16 defence in toxic psychosis cases without evidence of underlying disease of the mind.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds no evidence of underlying disorder; rejects appellant's assumption; no precedent for s.16 defence without such evidence.

propositions.text: Courts will face more difficult cases where mental disorder and drug-triggered toxic psychosis coexist.
How to apply legal characterization when toxic psychosis triggered by drugs but underlying disorder present.
Courts should apply Stone's 'more holistic approach' meticulously in such complex cases.

paragraphs.summary: The court notes future cases with underlying disorder and drug-triggered psychosis require careful application of Stone's holistic approach.

propositions.text: Whether s.33.1 Cr. C. applies in this case.
s.33.1 applies if accused was intoxicated, intoxication self-induced, and accused departed from reasonable care standard by threatening bodily integrity.
References to R. v. Vickberg and R. v. Chaulk for s.33.1 application principles.
If these conditions met, lack of general intent or voluntariness is not a defence.

paragraphs.summary: The court states s.33.1 applies if accused was self-intoxicated and threatened bodily integrity, negating intent defence.

propositions.text: Self-induced intoxication under s.33.1 is limited to period substance produces effects.
s.33.1(2) states person is criminally at fault if in self-induced intoxication state and interferes with bodily integrity.
s.33.1 prevents accused avoiding liability by claiming intoxication negated mental element or voluntariness.

paragraphs.summary: The court explains s.33.1 covers self-induced intoxication period and prevents intoxication negating criminal liability.

propositions.text: s.33.1 applies to any mental condition directly extending from intoxication.
Appellant wrongly suggests s.33.1 applies only to 'normal effects' of intoxication.
No intoxication threshold excludes s.33.1 application; toxic psychosis can be covered.
Toxic psychosis is covered by s.33.1 in this case.
Court of Appeal correctly held s.33.1 applicable rather than s.16 Cr. C.

paragraphs.summary: The court rejects appellant's narrow view of s.33.1, finds toxic psychosis covered, and affirms Court of Appeal's holding.

propositions.text: Appeal is dismissed.
Solicitors for appellant, respondent, and interveners are listed.

paragraphs.summary: The court dismisses the appeal and lists solicitors for parties and interveners.
